When you have enough information to act, act. Do not re-derive facts already established in the conversation, re-litigate a decision the user has already made, or narrate options you will not pursue. If you are weighing a choice, give a recommendation, not an exhaustive survey

The reasoning effort setting changes how much you think before you act. It does not change how much of the request you are expected to finish. A turn lasts as long as you keep working, so a large task can be finished in the turn where it was asked. The size of a task is not a reason to check in first.

Ending your turn stops all work until the user replies, and they may be away for a while. If you stop before changing anything, they come back to the same code they left, plus a message to read and answer. End your turn when the request is done or nothing is left that you can do without them.

Ask before you start only when you cannot name the most likely reading of the request. If you can name it, act on it, and say in your final message which reading you took. The other reason to ask first is that the whole task depends on a fact, a file, or access that only they have. Their approval of a choice you could make yourself is not one of these. Actions that are hard to reverse or outward-facing still need their confirmation. If they say they want to approve something before you go on, such as a plan, stop there. Words that only set an order, such as "plan, then build", are not a stopping point. Do each step and keep going. If they are asking a question or still deciding between options, they want your answer, not a change. If they also asked for work, answer and then do it.

The user can inspect and undo edits to files in the working tree. Such edits are not hard-to-reverse or outward-facing actions, unless they would overwrite changes the user has in progress. That leaves the open choices to you: how to build the change, how to split it up, how to handle a case the request did not cover. Pick what you would recommend, and keep to what the user wrote where they were specific. List your choices in the final message so the user can redirect you. Start editing once you know the first change. A design worked out in files persists, while a long stretch of thinking can be cut off and lost.

When one part of a task is blocked, unclear, or apparently wrong, the rest usually is not. If you suspect a step will fail, try it before you report it. Finish everything that does not depend on the stuck part, and open your final message with what is stuck. Finished parts are useful to the user even when the whole task is not done. Setting up the project so you can build and test it, such as installing its declared dependencies, is part of the work. If the code still cannot be built or run here, say so and make the changes you can verify by reading. If you investigate a problem and cannot find the cause, report what you ruled out and what would settle it. Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

14	const MS_PER_DAY = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;

16	export async function insertInvitation(
17	  orgId: OrgId,
18	  input: CreateInvitationInput,
19	  invitedBy: UserId,
20	  tokenHash: string,
21	): Promise<Invitation> {
22	  const stamp = toIsoTimestamp(new Date());
23	  const expiresAt = toIsoTimestamp(
24	    new Date(Date.now() + input.expiresInDays * MS_PER_DAY),
25	  );
26	
27	  const row = getDb()
28	    .insert(invitations)
29	    .values({
30	      id: newId(),
31	      orgId,
32	      email: input.email,
33	      role: input.role,
34	      invitedBy,
35	      tokenHash,
36	      expiresAt,
37	      acceptedAt: null,
38	      revokedAt: null,
39	      createdAt: stamp,
40	      updatedAt: stamp,
41	    })
42	    .returning()
43	    .get();
44	
45	  return toInvitation(row);

53	export async function findInvitationByTokenHash(
54	  tokenHash: string,
55	): Promise<Invitation | null> {
56	  const row = getDb()
57	    .select()
58	    .from(invitations)
59	    .where(eq(invitations.tokenHash, tokenHash))
60	    .get();
61	  return row ? toInvitation(row) : null;
62	}

64	export async function listPendingInvitations(
65	  orgId: OrgId,
66	): Promise<readonly Invitation[]> {
67	  const rows = getDb()
68	    .select()
69	    .from(invitations)
70	    .where(
71	      and(
72	        orgPredicate(invitations.orgId, orgId),
73	        isNull(invitations.acceptedAt),
74	        isNull(invitations.revokedAt),
75	      ),
76	    )
77	    .orderBy(desc(invitations.createdAt))
78	    .all();

127	  const row = getDb()

content.text:
The invitation lifecycle is designed, but this code does not complete it. Following the path from the members page, the invite call fails for every session before anything is written. Even if it passed, nothing creates a usable link or sends the mail. Below I walk through the path the code intends, marking where it breaks. This is from reading the code only; I did not run the test suite or a reproduction.

## 1. Checks before the invitation exists

`InviteMemberForm` (`src/components/domain/member/invite-member-form.tsx`) validates with `inviteMemberSchema` (`src/schemas/member.ts`) and submits `{orgId, email, role}` to `inviteMemberAction` (`src/actions/members/invite-member.ts`). That runs through `withAction` (`src/actions/_lib/with-action.ts`), in this order:

1. **Schema parse.** `emailSchema` (`src/schemas/common.ts`) validates the address and lowercases it. The role must be `admin`, `member` or `viewer` (`invitableRoleSchema`, `src/schemas/role.ts`). The `message` field passes validation and is then dropped.
2. **Actor resolution.** The input has `orgId` but no `orgSlug`, so `resolveActorFor` calls `requireActorFor` (`src/lib/actor.ts`). That requires a session principal from `getSessionPrincipal` (`src/lib/session.ts`) with a non-null `activeOrgId`, followed by a membership check in `resolveActorForOrg` (`src/server/services/session-service.ts`).
3. **Permission.** `can(actor, "member:invite", …)` in `src/lib/permissions.ts`. The matrix requires `admin`.
4. **Rate limit.** `consumeRateLimit(orgId, "member:invite")` (`src/lib/rate-limit.ts`), cost 1.
5. **Seat pre-check.** `getOrganizationSummary` reads the cached `organization_usage.seatsUsed`, which counts active members only.
6. **Service checks.** `inviteMember` delegates to `inviteMembers` (`src/server/services/invitation-service.ts`). It runs `assertOrgScope`, `assertCan` again, a second rate-limit charge of N, and the authoritative seat check: active members plus pending invitations, against `wouldExceedLimit` (`src/config/plan-limits.ts`).

Nothing checks whether the address already belongs to an active member, whether a pending invitation for it already exists, or whether a user with that address exists at all.

**The blocker is step 2.** `createSession` (`src/server/repositories/session-repository.ts`) always inserts `activeOrgId: null`. The only writer of that column is `setActiveOrg`, and nothing calls it. `switchActiveOrg` only validates, and `switchOrgAction` calls `requireActorFor` first, which fails when `activeOrgId` is null. So `requireActorFor` throws `NoMembershipError` for every session, and `inviteMemberAction` returns a forbidden result before any row is written. Pages that resolve the org from the slug (`loadTenantContext` → `getActor`) don't read the column, so they still render.

## 2. What is stored, and what would travel in the link

For each invitee, `inviteMembers` calls `randomToken(32)` (`src/lib/hash.ts`), which gives 32 random bytes as base64url (43 characters). `insertInvitation` (`src/server/repositories/invitation-repository.ts`) stores only `hashToken(token)`, an unsalted SHA-256 hex digest, in `invitations.token_hash`, which has a unique index (`src/server/db/schema/members.ts`). The row also holds `org_id`, the lowercased email, the role, `invited_by`, `expires_at` (now + 14 days), `accepted_at`, `revoked_at` and timestamps. No plaintext token is stored.

The raw token is never returned or emitted. The `member.invited` event carries the org, actor, email and role. The `Invitation` returned to the caller has a field named `token`, but `toInvitation` (`src/server/repositories/_mappers.ts`) fills it from `row.tokenHash`, so it holds the hash.

The intended link is `/invite/<token>`, served by `src/app/(auth)/invite/[token]/page.tsx`. It would carry only the token, and the tenant would come from the stored row. But nothing builds that URL. `InviteEmail` (`src/emails/invite-email.tsx`) takes an `acceptUrl`, yet `renderTemplate` in `src/emails/render.ts` has no production caller, and the invitation path never sends mail. The raw token goes out of scope when `inviteMembers` returns. The invitation tests seed rows directly with `hashToken(rawToken)`, so the round trip from invite to accept is never exercised.

## 3. Checks when the link is used

- `src/proxy.ts` treats `/invite` as a public prefix, so the page is reachable without a session cookie.
- The page checks the token's shape with `invitationTokenSchema`. With no session, it redirects to `/login?next=/invite/<token>`, dropping any `org` parameter. `safeDestination` in `src/app/(auth)/login/page.tsx` accepts only same-site paths.
- Signed in, `InviteAcceptForm` calls `acceptInvitationAction` (`src/actions/members/accept-invitation.ts`). It parses `acceptInvitationTokenSchema`, gets the principal, and calls `acceptInvitation(userId, input)` in the invitation service. That function:
  1. Looks up `findInvitationByTokenHash(hashToken(token))`. This is the one unscoped read, and the comment says the token carries the tenant.
  2. Rejects a revoked invitation, then an accepted one, then an expired one.
  3. If the user is already an active member (`findMember`), returns that member and leaves the invitation pending.
  4. Otherwise calls `insertMember` with the invitation's role and `invited_by`, then `markInvitationAccepted`, then emits `member.joined`.

  Nothing compares `invitation.email` with the signed-in user's address. The page shows the signed-in address as the one being added. The token alone is the credential, so a forwarded link works for whoever opens it.
- Back in the action, `assertSeatAvailable` calls `resolveActor` and then rejects if `usage.seatsUsed > limit`. That check runs after the member row, the `accepted_at` update and the usage increment are already written. No transaction wraps these writes anywhere in `src/`. If the check fails, the user sees "run out of seats", but the membership exists.
- On success the client pushes to `/orgs`, since no link carries `org`.

## 4. What the rest of the system learns

`member.joined` (actor is the new user) reaches these subscribers:

- `usage-service.ts`, in `registerUsageListeners`, increments the cached `seatsUsed` by one. This is a read-modify-write, not atomic.
- `notification-service.ts` writes an in-app notification to the organization owner (`org.ownerId`), with the joiner's raw user id in the body. The row records the email channel, but this path does not send mail immediately.

Nothing else reacts. `activity-service` subscribes only to `member.invited`, so the join is never in the activity feed. `webhook-service` has no `member.joined` subscriber, even though the event name is in `webhookEventTypeSchema`, so webhook endpoints never receive it. The search service ignores member events. The inviter is not notified. There is no welcome email, since that exists only on registration. The accept action does not call `revalidateTagged`, unlike the invite action.

In the database, the join leaves a `members` row with status `active`, the invitation's role, and `invited_by`, plus `accepted_at` on the invitation. From the next request on, `resolveActorForOrg` resolves the membership for each page load and writes `last_seen_at`. `can()` uses the stored role. `listOrgsForUser` joins on membership, so the workspace appears in the org list. The member is counted by the active-member count and by the usage counter.

## 5. Other problems I found

- **Expired invitations hold seats.** `countPendingInvitations` and `listPendingInvitations` filter on accepted and revoked only, not expiry. Nothing sweeps them. The UI's `isPending` hides expired rows, so the page can say "No pending invitations" while the seat count still includes them.
- **Re-joining after removal would fail.** `findMember` ignores archived rows, but `archiveMember` keeps the row, and `members_org_user_idx` is unique on `(org_id, user_id)`. The insert would violate that index, and the invitation would stay pending.
- **Duplicates and existing members are allowed.** The invite path doesn't check for an existing member or an existing invitation, and the email index is not unique. Each duplicate consumes a seat. Accepting as an existing member returns silently and leaves the invitation pending.
- **Rate limit is charged twice.** The action charges 1, and the service charges N for the same invite.
- **Seat display disagrees with enforcement.** The members page banner and form use the active-only counter, so the form can look available while the service refuses because of pending invitations.
- **Signed-out invitees dead-end.** The login page has no link to registration, the register page ignores `next`, and registration always creates a new workspace rather than consuming the invitation.
- **Smaller issues.** `resendInvitation` is not wired to any action. It revokes the old invitation before issuing the new one, so a failed reissue loses the original. `createInvitationSchema.expiresInDays` is ignored, since the service hard-codes 14 days. `acceptInvitationSchema` in `src/schemas/member.ts` is unused, and the comment in `src/actions/auth/register.ts` claims a transaction that does not exist.

To confirm the blocker without reading further, call `inviteMemberAction` with a session created by `createSession`. I expect a forbidden result, and I have not run that check.
